suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, and the result of the FlagSqlExpressions check is discarded. WHY: the feature flag has no effect, so SQL expressions stay disabled even when it is enabled, and the inverted `enabled` variable hides that. HOW: if the hard disable is intended, return false with a comment and drop the flag lookup. Otherwise return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions negates the flag into `enabled` and then returns false on both paths, so the computed value is never used. SQL expressions are rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Return the flag's actual value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Callers that could use SQL expressions with the flag on now always get an error. Return the flag's actual value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions reads as 'is the SQL expressions feature enabled', but the local `enabled` is the negation of the flag and both branches return false. The function is constant-false, so the name and variable misstate the behavior and the flag has no effect. Return the flag value directly, or rename the function and variable to say that SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path. The flag is negated into `enabled`, and the fallthrough also returns false. SQL expressions are therefore rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Return the flag's value directly.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path: the `enabled` variable is inverted and both branches return false. The feature flag therefore has no effect, and every SQL expression query fails to parse with "not implemented". Return the flag's actual value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. WHY: a cached denial for one resource can wrongly deny a different resource the user is permitted to access, for example (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c'). HOW: use a separator that cannot appear in names, or length-prefix or hash the name and parent components.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says access to the dashboard is allowed, but the permCache entry is set to false (`dashboards:uid:dash1: false`). A map value of false does not grant access, so the test does not prove that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to true so the code matches the comment.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The deny-cache test is meant to show that the denial entry overrides cached permissions, but the permCache entry is set to false. That value denies anyway, so the test passes even if the permDenialCache check is deleted. Set the cached permission to true so the test fails unless the denial entry short-circuits Check.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Debug logging at Error level on every batch dumps the full ID slice and the condition, and does so even when there is no error. WHY: Each cleanup batch emits large error-level log lines (up to batch-size IDs), which floods the logs and falsely triggers error alerting. HOW: Remove these r.log.Error calls, or log only the counts at Debug level.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. WHY: The whole cleanup job, including annotation cleanup, now runs 10x as often, so heavy deletes can run back-to-back against a 9-minute job timeout and increase DB load and lock contention. HOW: Restore the original `time.Minute * 10` interval.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: Debug-style r.log.Error calls dump the full list of annotation IDs and the raw SQL condition on every cleanup batch, even on success. This leaks internal record identifiers and query text into error-level logs and can create enormous log lines with large batch sizes. Remove these calls, or log only counts at debug level. The same pattern is repeated in the max-count cleanup and in CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Routine progress messages such as "Annotations to clean by time" and "cleaned annotations by time" are logged with r.log.Error, so the level contradicts the message content. The "err", err value logged right after the err != nil check is always nil. The same pattern appears in the count-based and orphaned-tag cleanup paths. Use Debug or Info and drop the always-nil err field.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says SQLite has a parameter limit of 999, but the new test is named for SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER on SQLite >= 3.32.0, where the limit is 32766. The comment and the 999 constant therefore describe only older SQLite versions. Reword the comment to say the 999 limit applies to older SQLite versions, or correct the threshold.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Normal cleanup batches are logged with r.log.Error, including the full ids slice, and err is logged even when nil. This produces false error alerts and huge log lines (batch sizes up to 32767). The same pattern appears at lines 554-557 and 576-579. Remove these debug logs or log them at Debug level without the ids.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The cleanup job interval was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no related reason. It looks like a debugging leftover, and it makes every cleanup task run ten times as often. Restore the 10 minute interval.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readInteger and readNext pass it straight to read(int), which allocates `new byte[-1]`. WHY: a malformed or indefinite-length DER signature throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of the IOException that callers expect. HOW: reject negative lengths in read(int) or in the callers by throwing an IOException.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `order()` is added as an abstract method with no default implementation. WHY: every other CryptoProvider implementation outside this PR's module updates stops compiling, and any provider already compiled against the old interface throws AbstractMethodError when `order()` is called during the sort in CryptoIntegration. HOW: make it a default method, for example `default int order() { return 0; }`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: These two lines encode r and s into temporary ASN1Encoder instances and discard the results. The return statement then re-encodes the same values in new encoders, so the work is dead computation and should be removed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented in the CryptoProvider interface as returning the BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the JDK default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN). Callers that rely on the name will get a non-BC provider. Either document the deviation on this override or return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does when it has no BC.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The test only compares rsConcat with its own round trip, so a consistently wrong encoder and decoder would still pass. Also assert that the re-encoded DER equals the original `sign`, or verify the re-encoded signature with Signature.initVerify.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The default "EC" key is P-256 for all algorithms, so ES384 and ES512 never exercise 384-bit or 521-bit r/s sizes. Generate the key pair with the curve matching each algorithm (secp384r1, secp521r1).

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: integerToBytes silently truncates r/s values longer than the curve size, so malformed or non-canonical DER signatures are accepted as a different valid-looking value (signature malleability). Reject values that exceed qLength after stripping a single leading sign byte instead of truncating.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: canManage() grants manage access when the caller only holds the VIEW scope on all groups, because it checks VIEW and MANAGE together. WHY: an admin with view-only permission on groups can create groups, update groups and map roles to them, which is privilege escalation. HOW: check only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: searchForUser no longer filters results with usersEvaluator::canView, and the group restriction is now applied only when the group id set is non-empty. WHY: an admin who can query users but has no view permission and no group grants has an empty group set, so the search may return every user in the realm. HOW: keep the per-user filter, e.g. `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)`, on the search stream.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission iterates every group resource and runs a full permission evaluation for each one. WHY: it is called on every user search and user count for non-global viewers, so the cost grows as O(groups) policy evaluations per request. HOW: evaluate permissions once for the scopes across the Groups resource type and collect the matching resources, or cache the result per request.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only a view permission on all groups is treated as able to manage groups. This disagrees with canManage(GroupModel), which checks MANAGE only. Check only MANAGE here.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Javadoc for requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws when canManageMembership returns false. The method is about members, so the doc should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the 'view' scope on all groups passes the manage check. This breaks the documented contract (manage requires the MANAGE scope) and lets view-only admins create or modify groups. Check only the MANAGE scope.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The per-user `usersEvaluator::canView` filter was removed from user search. The search is now limited only by the GROUPS session attribute, which is set only when the caller has group view grants. A caller with query access but no view permission and no group grants may therefore get an unrestricted user list, exposing user data. Keep the per-user canView filter (or confirm that toRepresentation enforces it).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: An empty set from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is now indistinguishable from 'caller may view everything'. When the caller cannot view users and has no viewable groups, UserModel.GROUPS is never set. The search then runs unrestricted, and the removed `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` no longer catches it. Restore the per-user canView filter, or explicitly return no results when canView() is false and the set is empty.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns an empty set both for 'can view all users' and for 'no viewable groups'. searchForUser now sets no group restriction when the set is empty and no longer applies usersEvaluator::canView. A caller who can only query, or who has per-user view permission, may therefore get unfiltered search results. Keep the per-user canView filter, or restore the canView() guard so the empty set is only treated as 'unrestricted' for callers who can view all users.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The plaintext recovery codes (generatedCodes) are serialized to JSON and sent to the user storage provider via updateCredential. The local path stores only the hashed credentialModel. WHY: Any federated or external store that accepts the credential now holds usable one-time recovery codes in clear text, which weakens the hashing the local path provides. HOW: Pass the hashed credential data (the credentialModel's credential data) to user storage, or confirm the user storage contract explicitly requires plaintext codes and document it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The credential is now looked up with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which can return a federated credential. The code after it still handles the credential as a local one (it updates or removes the used code through local stored-credential APIs). WHY: When recovery codes live in user storage, consuming a code may fail or touch the wrong store, so used codes are not invalidated or login throws. HOW: Make the consume/update step in this authenticator work with the credential's actual source, using the user storage update path for federated credentials.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The plaintext recovery codes are serialized to JSON and passed to the user storage provider's updateCredential. The local path stores only hashed codes, so the user-storage path exposes raw one-time secrets to external systems, which may persist or log them. Send hashed or derived credential data to federated storage, or restrict this to providers explicitly trusted to protect secrets.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: getCredential() can now return a credential that lives in user storage, but the code that follows still removes an exhausted credential with removeStoredCredentialById(), which only affects the local DB. For a federated credential, once all codes are used the removal is a no-op and the stale credential stays in user storage. Route the removal through a user-storage-aware path, matching how creation now works.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative start offset taken directly from the user-supplied cursor. WHY: Django querysets raise ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so a crafted cursor such as `0:-5:0` returns a 500 instead of a 400. HOW: reject negative offsets (raise BadPaginationError or clamp with max(0, offset)) and remove the negative-offset branch.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: BasePaginator.get_result still passes the raw negative offset to the queryset slice whenever cursor.is_prev is true. WHY: This affects every paginated endpoint, and a user-supplied prev cursor with a negative offset raises ValueError (500). The added comment wrongly says the queryset handles boundaries. HOW: clamp or reject negative offsets for all cursors.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every request, even when optimized_pagination is not set, and `member` can be None. WHY: A non-superuser whose member is None raises AttributeError and breaks the audit log endpoint that previously worked. HOW: evaluate the check only when use_optimized is true and guard against a None member.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: A user-supplied cursor offset flows unchecked into a negative queryset slice when enable_advanced_features is set. Django rejects negative indexing with an unhandled AssertionError, so a crafted cursor produces a 500 with internal error detail, and the intent of the code is to reach rows beyond normal pagination bounds. Clamp the offset to >= 0 and reject negative cursor offsets.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The advanced path slices the queryset with a negative start (cursor.offset < 0), but Django querysets do not support negative slice indices and raise ValueError. A client-supplied cursor with a negative offset plus optimized_pagination=true therefore causes a 500, or out-of-bounds reads if the queryset were a list. Clamp the offset to >= 0 or reject negative offsets when the cursor is parsed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The clamp `max(0, offset)` is skipped when cursor.is_prev is true, so a negative offset from a crafted prev cursor is passed directly as the slice start in BasePaginator.get_result. Django rejects negative slicing, so this raises ValueError and returns a 500 for every paginated endpoint. Always clamp the offset to >= 0.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The negative-offset branch claims Django ORM handles negative slicing, but QuerySet slicing with a negative start raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). A request with a negative cursor offset and optimized_pagination=true therefore errors instead of paginating in reverse. Clamp the offset to 0 as the else branch does, and drop the misleading claim.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comments claim Django ORM handles negative slicing and that permissions are checked at the queryset level, so negative offsets are safe.
